input.candidate_text:
Let \(p\equiv1\pmod4\) be any prime with \(p\nmid y\). Choose \(a\not\equiv0\pmod p\) such that
\[
(ay)^2\equiv-1\pmod p;
\]
such an \(a\) exists because \(-1\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(p\).

Write \(p-1=2^e s\), where \(e\ge2\) and \(s\) is odd. By the Chinese remainder theorem, choose \(b\) satisfying
\[
b\equiv3\pmod{2^e},\qquad b\equiv2\pmod{q^v}
\]
for every odd prime power \(q^v\mid p-1\). Then
\[
\gcd(b,p-1)=1,\qquad \gcd(b-1,p-1)=2.
\]
Again by the Chinese remainder theorem, choose \(r\) such that
\[
r\equiv a\pmod p,
\qquad r\equiv b\pmod{p-1}.
\]
Since \(\gcd(r,p(p-1))=1\), Dirichlet's theorem gives a prime \(\ell\) with
\[
\ell\equiv r\pmod{p(p-1)}.
\]
Thus \(\ell\equiv a\pmod p\), so
\[
p\mid (\ell y)^2+1.
\]
Applying the hypothesis with \(n=\ell\), and using \(\varphi(\ell)=\ell-1\), gives
\[
p\mid x^{\ell-1}-1.
\]
In particular \(p\nmid x\). If \(d=\operatorname{ord}_p(x)\), then
\[
d\mid \ell-1\quad\text{and}\quad d\mid p-1.
\]
Moreover, \(\ell\equiv b\pmod{p-1}\), hence
\[
\gcd(\ell-1,p-1)=\gcd(b-1,p-1)=2.
\]
Therefore \(d\mid2\), and consequently
\[
x^2\equiv1\pmod p.
\]

There are infinitely many primes \(p\equiv1\pmod4\), and only finitely many divide \(y\). Hence infinitely many primes divide the fixed integer \(x^2-1\). This is possible only if \(x^2-1=0\). Since \(x\) is positive, \(x=1\).

problem.theorem:
Let \( x \) and \( y \) be positive integers. If for each positive integer \( n \) we have that

\[
(n y)^{2}+1 \mid x^{\varphi(n)}-1
\]

prove that \( x=1 \).
